> **Beta.** HTTP mode is new in this release, and no client has used it day to day yet. It passes its full test suite against the pinned JDT LS 1.63.0. Expect rough edges, and report them as [issues](https://github.com/nokesc/fractal-jdtls/issues). The API is versioned (`/v1/`, API version 1.0.0), but its operations and their fields may still change before a non-beta release.

The second release of Fractal JDT LS. It pins the same Eclipse JDT Language Server 1.63.0 and Byte Buddy as `v1.63.0-1`, and the launcher and agent behave as before. What's new is an opt-in **HTTP mode**, which lets several sessions, each in its own Git worktree of a Maven project, share one JDT LS process through a JSON API.

**Linux only.** Needs Python 3.10 or newer and a JDK 21 or newer (for HTTP mode, a Java with the `jdk.httpserver` module, which every full JDK has). See the [README](https://github.com/nokesc/fractal-jdtls#readme) for installing and using it.

## HTTP mode

Start the launcher with `--http-port-file <file>`, and a token in `FRACTAL_JDTLS_HTTP_TOKEN`:

```bash
export FRACTAL_JDTLS_HTTP_TOKEN="$(python3 -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))')"
jdtls -data <workspace> --http-port-file <file> [--http-settings <settings.json>]
```

The launcher then also loads this release's endpoint, an OSGi bundle in `lib/fractal-jdtls-endpoint.jar`. It becomes JDT LS's only client, connected inside the JVM, and serves a REST API on `127.0.0.1`. Once it's listening, it writes `{"port", "pid", "release", "api"}` to the port file. `--http-settings` passes the LSP settings, as one JSON object. Stop it with `POST /v1/shutdown`, or by killing the process you started. Without `--http-port-file`, nothing changes.

- **The API** is JSON over HTTP/1.1, under `/v1/`, API version 1.0.0. Its contract is an OpenAPI 3.1 description, served at `GET /v1/openapi.json`, with every operation, error code and example, written to be read by an LLM.
- **Worktrees** are added and removed at runtime (`/v1/worktrees/add`, `/remove`, `/list`). Each import's health is checked, and a broken one is repaired once, or reported. The registered worktrees come back on a restart with the same `-data`.
- **Every operation names its worktree and Maven module,** never Eclipse's project names, and its results never come from another worktree.
- **The disk is the truth.** Sessions edit files with their own tools, `git checkout` or `sed`, and don't tell the endpoint. Before every operation on code, it reconciles JDT LS with the disk: it refreshes the worktree, sends changed POMs through m2e, runs a build and joins Eclipse's jobs, with no file watcher and no timing. When nothing changed, a fast check skips all that. Changes that keep a file's modification time (`cp -p`, `touch -r`) are found too. Every answer reports what was found in `sync`.
- **Builds and problems** (`/v1/build`, `/v1/problems`) come from Eclipse's markers, never from cached diagnostics.
- **Navigation by Java name** (`com.acme.Foo#bar(int)`), or by a text anchor for code without a name: definition, references, implementations, type and call hierarchies, outline, symbols, and `describe` (a signature and its Javadoc), including JDK and Maven library names.
- **Refactorings:** rename (of a type with its file, a method, field, local variable or package), organize imports, extract local variable, constant and method, and inline local variable. Each one is checked against the files it was computed from before anything is written, written all or nothing, built, and returned as a unified diff. A dry run returns the diff and a `writeSetDigest`, which an apply can require. Each refactoring is recorded in `<worktree>/temp/fractal-jdtls/<id>/`: its request, its diff and its answer.
- **An LSP passthrough,** `POST /v1/lsp`, for anything else JDT LS serves, with LSP's own URIs and positions.
- **Concurrency:** reads run at once, on 16 worker threads with 64 requests queued. Operations that change the workspace run one at a time under Eclipse's workspace rule. Every operation has a timeout, which cancels the LSP request or the Eclipse work. A request the endpoint can't take now gets `busy` with `retryAfter`. Errors are RFC 9457 problems, each with a stable `code`, a `hint` and, when there's a choice, `candidates` that can be sent straight back.

### Security

- **Localhost only.** The endpoint listens only on `127.0.0.1`, on a port the kernel picks. There's no TLS, because the traffic never leaves the machine.
- **A bearer token on every request,** compared in constant time. A missing or wrong one gets `401`, with no detail. The token must be 32 to 4,096 visible ASCII characters. It's never on a command line: the launcher hands it to the endpoint through a pipe and removes it from the environment, so neither JDT LS nor anything it starts, such as Maven, has it. It's never logged.
- **No browser can reach it.** `Host` must be `127.0.0.1:<port>`, and a request with an `Origin` header is refused, which stops DNS rebinding.
- **LSP never leaves the process.** The endpoint talks to JDT LS through pipes on the Java heap: there's no socket or file descriptor another process could open. In HTTP mode, the launcher never passes JDT LS's other transports, and starts it with stdin from `/dev/null`.
- **The port file is mode 0600,** written atomically once the endpoint listens. It's removed on a clean shutdown.
- **A caller without the token can't hold a worker thread.** The JDK HTTP server's limits bound slow and idle connections: 10 s to send a request, and at most 256 connections.
- **Writes stay in the worktree.** A refactoring never writes outside its worktree's real root, symbolic links resolved, and the passthrough refuses a request whose `file:` or `jdt:` URIs point at another worktree.

## What's pinned

Unchanged from `v1.63.0-1`: only the release's ID changed in `pin.json`.

| Component | Version | Verified against |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Eclipse JDT LS | 1.63.0 (`jdt-language-server-1.63.0-202610191322.tar.gz`) | SHA-256 `b1f2abe0b3cccb462cf64fb4a5587c7d09df60cf8be7748b152cbd89d018bdc4`, equal to Eclipse's published `.sha256`; plus the SHA-256 of each of its 124 files |
| m2e (bundled in JDT LS) | core `2.8.0.20260815-0704`, jdt `2.5.300.20260813-1359`, embedded Maven `3.9.16` | the tarball's checksum only (see below) |
| Byte Buddy | 1.18.14, from Maven Central | SHA-256 `b7f2b2f111c6ddc09d3d9718ca5895dde16217bb4e5f2d2a6eb571f274909a82`, equal to Central's published `.sha512`, `.sha256` and `.sha1` |
| Java | 21 or newer, JDT LS 1.63.0's minimum | the launcher refuses an older one |

The zip holds only this project's files: `bin/install.py`, `bin/jdtls`, the agent and boot jars, the endpoint's jar and HTTP mode's Eclipse preferences (`lib/http-mode-preferences.ini`), `pin.json`, `release-files.json`, `LICENSE` and `NOTICE`. The endpoint adds no third-party code: HTTP comes from the JDK, and JSON from the Gson bundled in JDT LS. The installer downloads JDT LS from `download.eclipse.org` and Byte Buddy from Maven Central, and verifies every file before installing. Nothing from Eclipse or Byte Buddy is redistributed.

Tested together: the agent's and the endpoint's JUnit tests, the installer's and launcher's unit tests, a check of the OpenAPI description, and an integration suite that installs this zip and runs real JDT LS 1.63.0 on a main checkout and linked worktrees of one Maven project. Without HTTP mode, each worktree resolves its own modules after import, edits, reimport and restart, and without the agent the same fixture fails with m2e's duplicate-coordinates error. In HTTP mode, through HTTP only, the suite runs every operation, edits made on disk and never reported, each refactoring applied and built, four sessions at once in different worktrees, timeouts and a full queue, and a generated tree of 51 Maven projects and 10,001 Java files.

## How each downloaded file is trusted

`pin.json` holds the SHA-256 of every file, so an install can be re-checked at any time (`install.py --verify`), and the launcher checks it on every start. What each file *should* be comes from outside checks, recorded in the [pin report](https://github.com/nokesc/fractal-jdtls/blob/v1.63.0-2/.context/pins/1.63.0.md):

- **Eclipse signs only some of JDT LS.** 58 of the 110 jars in `plugins/`, and the one jar in `features/`, are signed by the Eclipse Foundation (`jarsigner -verify`).
- **41 jars are byte-identical to artifacts on Maven Central.**
- **Eclipse publishes no PGP signature for the tarball,** only its SHA-256.
- **29 jars and 13 other files are trusted only through that checksum.** Nothing else vouches for them:
  - all of m2e: `org.eclipse.m2e.core`, `org.eclipse.m2e.jdt`, `org.eclipse.m2e.maven.runtime` and `org.eclipse.m2e.apt.core`. This m2e build isn't on m2e's signed update sites.
  - `com.sun.jna_5.19.1.v20260612-1000`, `org.eclipse.jdt.core.javac_1.0.0.z20260430-1959` and the wrapped decompiler engine;
  - 21 wrapped flexmark jars and `wrapped.org.jetbrains.annotations`;
  - the scripts and configuration: `bin/jdtls`, `bin/jdtls.bat`, `bin/jdtls.py` and the ten `config_*/config.ini` files. The launcher never runs Eclipse's `bin/jdtls` scripts; it uses `config_linux/config.ini` as JDT LS's shared configuration.
- **Byte Buddy's PGP signature (`.asc`) wasn't checked when it was pinned:** the signer's key (`7999BEFBA1039E8B`) wasn't in the maintainer's keyring. Byte Buddy is trusted through Maven Central's published hashes.

## Known gaps

- **The agent must be present on every start.** A workspace created without it keeps its projects' unprefixed names, and resolves across worktrees again. To start using the agent with an existing workspace, give JDT LS a fresh `-data`.
- **Worktree folder names must be unique** among the worktrees that share one JDT LS process. Projects are named `<worktree folder>.<artifactId>`. In HTTP mode, adding a worktree whose folder name is in use is refused; otherwise the agent reports a collision but can't resolve it.
- **Version-pinned internals.** The agent hooks private methods of m2e and Maven in this JDT LS build, and the endpoint relies on some of JDT LS's and m2e's internals. The agent reports any hook that isn't in place, and the endpoint refuses to start if the internals it can check have changed, but a different JDT LS needs a new release of this project.
- **The refactorings are the ones listed above.** Move, change signature, quick fixes, source generation, and Eclipse's refactorings that JDT LS doesn't expose (pull up, push down, encapsulate field) are still to come.
- **The LSP passthrough** sends only requests it has classified as safe, and refuses those that would change projects, settings or open documents behind the endpoint's back, and those whose URIs point outside the named worktree. It doesn't filter results: they're JDT LS's own, with its URIs and 0-based positions.
- **A worktree change runs alone.** While a worktree is added or removed, other requests that reach JDT LS wait for it, or get `not-ready` with `retryAfter`. Adding the generated tree of 51 projects took about 8 seconds.
- **A caller that disconnects isn't noticed.** Its work goes on until its `timeoutMs`, and is cancelled then. Send a `timeoutMs` no longer than you'll wait.
- **A refactoring isn't a transaction.** If JDT LS is killed while it writes, some files can be left edited; Git is the undo. Its record in `temp/fractal-jdtls/<id>/` names the files, and a missing `response.json` means its outcome is unknown.
- **Measured only on WSL2's ext4,** on the test fixture and the generated tree. Before every operation on code, the whole worktree is checked against the disk, and refreshed and built if anything changed: about half a second either way on the generated tree. WSL2's `/mnt` paths, larger reactors and many worktrees aren't measured.
- Linux only. Gradle, classifiers and version ranges aren't tested.

Report a problem: <https://github.com/nokesc/fractal-jdtls/issues>.
